How fast could you get through it? According to the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation, lawmakers had just 13 hours to read 1,100 pages of material that would cost the American taxpayer $787 billion. That's less than a minute and a half per page, with no time for bathroom breaks. No wonder so many of our lawmakers didn't seem to notice that last-minute exemption clearing the way for bailed-out companies like AIG to pay out big bonuses. So, the House tried to clean up the mess last week by rushing through another bill -- a tax on AIG bonuses. That bill was just 11 hours old before it went on the floor to be argued and then quickly approved. And the list goes on well before the president took office. The bank bailout got all of 29 hours, the rescue of Fannie and Freddie was only available for 19 hours. This is how bills could literally become, to borrow a phrase, too big to fail -- and too fast to stop. The Sunlight Foundation is calling on Congress to allow the American people three days, 72 hours, to read a nonemergency bill online before debate begins. We strongly agree. And yes lawmakers, you can have three days to read it over, too, before taking a stand. As for President Obama's promise of a five-day public review once a bill leaves Capitol Hill headed for his desk, it would be nice if he kept his word on this going forward. ***

**Editor's note:** *Campbell Brown anchors CNN's "Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull" at 8 p.m. ET, Monday through Friday. She delivered this commentary during the "Cutting through the Bull" segment of Monday night's broadcast.*

**(CNN) —** Whether through omission or commission, both the White House and Congress bear responsibility for failing to uphold the new era of transparency promised by President Obama. 

The president’s former campaign website explicitly stated this commitment for all to see: *"As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House Web site for five days."*

However, President Obama breached that promise barely a week after taking office when he signed the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act. While it was a commendable piece of legislation, it certainly could have accommodated a five-day public comment period. Perhaps the White House simply forgot?

Then there is Congress and the Stimulus Bill. How quickly could anyone truly digest such a document? According to the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation, lawmakers were given a mere 13 hours to review 1,100 pages of legislation carrying a $787 billion price tag for American taxpayers. That amounts to less than a minute and a half per page—leaving virtually no time for pause, let alone thorough comprehension.

It is hardly surprising, then, that so many lawmakers failed to notice a last-minute exemption permitting bailed-out corporations, such as AIG, to distribute massive executive bonuses. In an attempt to rectify this oversight last week, the House rushed to pass corrective legislation: a tax on AIG bonuses. That bill had been finalized for a mere 11 hours before reaching the House floor for debate and swift approval.

This pattern of haste, however, precedes the current administration. The bank bailout received just 29 hours of review, while the rescue plan for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac was available for only 19 hours. In this manner, legislation risks becoming—to borrow a phrase—"too big to fail" and too fast to stop.

To address this issue, the Sunlight Foundation is urging Congress to grant the American public three days—72 hours—to review nonemergency legislation online before debate begins. We strongly endorse this proposal. Lawmakers, too, deserve those three days to fully digest the material before taking a stand. 

As for President Obama’s pledge to allow a five-day public review once a bill leaves Capitol Hill, he would do well to honor his word moving forward.

*The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Campbell Brown.*

# The Illusion of Transparency: How Rushed Legislation Became the Standard in Washington

Despite campaign promises to usher in a new era of open government, both President Barack Obama and leaders in Congress repeatedly failed to uphold their commitments to legislative transparency and public review during the early stages of his administration. Rather than fostering a deliberate and open lawmaking process, Washington established a troubling pattern of fast-tracking massive, high-stakes bills through the legislative pipeline before either the public or lawmakers could properly evaluate them.

This departure from promised transparency occurred almost immediately. During his 2008 campaign, President Obama repeatedly pledged to post non-emergency legislation online for a five-day public review period before signing it into law. However, he violated this explicit promise with his very first legislative act. Shortly after taking office, President Obama signed the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act without providing the promised five-day window for public scrutiny, setting an early precedent for prioritizing speed over openness.

Congress exhibited the same disregard for meaningful review when crafting economic recovery policy. When the massive, 1,100-page American Recovery and Reinvestment Act—commonly known as the stimulus bill—was brought to a vote, lawmakers were given a mere 13 hours to read and analyze the complex document. The sheer impossibility of digesting such a massive amount of high-stakes legislation in half a day led directly to severe political and economic oversights. Most notably, lawmakers failed to catch a critical provision that explicitly exempted executives at American International Group (AIG) from restrictions on corporate bonuses. 

Rather than correcting course after the stimulus debacle, the House of Representatives continued the trend of hasty, reactive lawmaking. Facing severe public backlash over the newly revealed executive payouts, the House rushed to pass a targeted tax on AIG bonuses just 11 hours after the bill was introduced. Instead of engaging in thoughtful policy design, Congress opted for immediate, knee-jerk legislation to manage a public relations crisis caused by its own previous lack of scrutiny.

Ultimately, these episodes reflect a systemic problem in modern governance. The fast-tracking of multi-billion-dollar spending measures and bailout packages without adequate time for public or congressional review has evolved from an occasional necessity into a routine habit. Bypassing transparency in favor of speed undermines democratic accountability, deprives lawmakers of the ability to govern responsibly, and predictably leads to flawed legislation with far-reaching consequences.

**The High Cost of Haste: How Rushed Legislation Undermines American Governance**

In an era where political leaders frequently pledge allegiance to open government and civic engagement, the actual mechanics of lawmaking often tell a radically different story. Through a critical examination of several massive, fast-tracked bills, journalist Campbell Brown illuminates a troubling pattern in Washington: both the White House and Congress consistently fail to deliver on their promises of transparency. By pushing thousands of pages of complex legislation through the Capitol at breakneck speed, political leaders effectively deny both the public and lawmakers themselves the necessary time to read, evaluate, and debate the laws that govern the nation.

This practice of "legislating in the dark" relies on a toxic blend of political urgency and procedural sleight of hand. During times of national crisis or extreme partisan push, major legislative packages are frequently drafted behind closed doors, amended in the dead of night, and brought to the floor for a vote within hours of being finalized. Both executive leadership and congressional leaders often defend this frantic pace as an imperative of swift action. However, as Brown points out, this defense ignores the explicitly stated promises—often made during campaign cycles—that bills would be made available online for public review prior to a vote or executive signature. When lawmakers are forced to vote on mammoth packages without having read them, the constitutional ideal of deliberative democracy is replaced by mere political rubber-stamping.

The consequences of this rushed process extend far beyond abstract procedural debates; they manifest as tangible, high-stakes policy failures. When speed is prioritized over thorough oversight, massive legislative backdoors and unintended consequences slip through unnoticed. 

A prime example highlighted in Brown’s analysis occurred during the federal response to the 2008 financial crisis. As Congress scrambled to pass sweeping economic recovery packages, a crucial exemption was quietly inserted into a massive spending bill. Because lawmakers were granted virtually no time to scrutinize the final text before casting their votes, few realized that the language contained a specific loophole protecting pre-existing executive compensation agreements. This legal oversight enabled the insurance giant American International Group (AIG)—which had just received over $170 billion in taxpayer-funded bailout money—to distribute hundreds of millions of dollars in executive bonuses. The public outcry was swift, and politicians expressed loud indignation, yet the scandal was entirely self-inflicted: a direct byproduct of a legislative system that values velocity over vigilance.

Ultimately, Campbell Brown’s critique serves as a stark warning about the long-term health of democratic institutions. When legislative processes are routinely hurried, governance degrades, special interests exploit blind spots, and public trust in government erodes. Emergency mandates and political ambitions must not be allowed to override the fundamental requirement of rigorous legislative review. If Congress and the White House continue to sacrifice transparency on the altar of speed, the result will inevitably be bad policy, unmanageable oversights, and a citizenry increasingly alienated from its government.

Central to this creative explosion was the vital, often demanding role of the **editor**: a gatekeeper, mentor, and catalyst capable of turning a raw idea into a movement.

Few figures loom as large in editorial history as John W. **Campbell**. Taking the helm of *Astounding Science Fiction* in 1937, Campbell did not merely select stories for publication; he actively sculpted the genre itself. He challenged his writers to abandon cheap pulp clichés in favor of scientific plausibility, psychological depth, and complex societal themes. Under Campbell’s rigorous editorial eye, science fiction matured into a respected form of modern mythology. 

During this golden era, the magazine stands relied on versatile, sharp-witted authors like Fredric **Brown**. Master of the short story, the clever twist ending, and flash fiction, Brown brought a unique blend of humor, mystery, and existential dread to his work. Writers of Brown’s caliber navigated a publishing environment where pleasing an editor like Campbell meant pushing the boundaries of one's imagination while maintaining strict narrative logic and tight, economic prose. 

The relationship between a visionary **editor** and a brilliant writer is one of constructive tension. While Campbell provided the high-concept standard and high expectations, writers like Brown supplied the human wit, irony, and storytelling magic that resonated with readers. Together, through a continuous cycle of submissions, revisions, and bold ideas, editors and authors of that era built the foundation of modern science fiction—proving that great literature is rarely born in total solitude, but forged in the creative exchange between a writer's voice and an editor's vision.

**Segment:** *Cutting Through the Bull*  

> **CAMPBELL BROWN:** "Tonight, we are cutting through the bull on Congress and this rush to pass massive, complicated legislation without actually giving anyone time to read it.

>
> *(Video clip of candidate Barack Obama: 'When there's a bill that ends up on my desk as president, you the public will have five days to look online and find out what's in it before I sign it, so that you have a chance to vote your opinion and let your opinion be heard.')*

> **BROWN:** "Well, fast-forward to today. 
>
> Right now, Congress is trying to jam through massive, thousand-page pieces of legislation—bills that affect your healthcare, your taxes, your energy bills, and the national debt for generations to come. And how are they doing it? By handing out thousand-page documents in the middle of the night and demanding a vote just hours later. 
>
> Lawmakers themselves are admitting on camera that they haven't read the bill. How can you vote on a bill when you don't even know what's in it?

>

Here is the transcript excerpt from Campbell Brown’s show ***No Bias, No Bull*** on CNN, aired in **February 2009**. 

In this segment, Campbell Brown held President Barack Obama accountable for breaking a major campaign pledge regarding transparency and the 5-day public review rule for the $787 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (the Stimulus Bill).

***

### **CNN: CAMPBELL BROWN: NO BIAS, NO BULL**
**Air Date:** February 16, 2009  
**Topic:** President Obama’s Broken Transparency Promise on the Stimulus Bill  

**CAMPBELL BROWN (HOST):** Tonight, we are cutting through the spin on President Obama’s promise of transparency. 

During the campaign, Candidate Barack Obama made a very specific, very clear promise about how he would run the government. He pledged that before he signed any major piece of legislation, it would be posted on the White House website for five days so the American public could read it and see what was in it. 

Let’s listen to Candidate Obama in his own words.

> **BARACK OBAMA (ARCHIVAL CAMPAIGN FOOTAGE):** *"Too often, draft bills are written in the dark of night, pushed through Congress without public debate, and signed into law before anyone has a chance to read them. When I’m president, we will put those bills online for five days before I sign them, so you can see what’s in them and have your say."*

**BROWN:** Five days. Not four days, not three days—five days. It was a simple promise aimed at ending the Washington tradition of midnight deals and rushed votes. 

So, fast-forward to today. Congress passed the final version of the massive $787 billion economic stimulus bill—a document over 1,000 pages long—late on a Friday night. President Obama is scheduled to sign that bill tomorrow, Tuesday, in Denver. 

Mathematically, that is not five days. In fact, the final text was not made available on the White House website in a way that gives the public five full days to review it before it becomes law.

Today, White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs was pressed by reporters on why the President is violating his own campaign pledge on the very first major piece of legislation of his presidency. Here is how Gibbs tried to explain it.

> **REPORTER (PRESS BRIEFING):** *"The President promised on the campaign trail that he would leave bills on the website for five days before signing them. Why isn't he doing that with the stimulus bill?"*
>
> **ROBERT GIBBS (WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY):** *"Well, the bill has been posted online for days. People have had an opportunity to review it. The draft versions have been out there, and the public has been part of this process from the beginning. The President believes this urgency is required because of the state of the economy."*

**BROWN:** Okay, let’s be honest about what is happening here. That is classic political dodge. 

Yes, the economy is in bad shape. Yes, the administration feels a sense of urgency. But President Obama didn't say during the campaign, *"I will post bills for five days unless there's an emergency,"* or *"unless I really want to sign it quickly."* 

The entire point of the five-day rule was for moments *just like this*—when a massive, complicated, thousand-page bill spending nearly a trillion dollars of taxpayer money is rushed through Congress in the dead of night. 

If transparency only applies to minor, non-controversial bills when there's no rush, then the promise means nothing. 

Now, whether you support the stimulus bill or oppose it, process matters. Promises matter. President Obama made transparency a cornerstone of his campaign. Breaking that promise on his very first major legislative victory isn't just a minor oversight—it’s standard Washington business as usual. And that is where we see the bull.

**PROGRAM:** CNN NEWSROOM  
**SEGMENT:** CUTTING THROUGH THE BULL  
**HOST:** [Anchor Name]  
**TOPIC:** Government Transparency and the Broken Promises of Washington  

---

**[GRAPHIC ON SCREEN: CUTTING THROUGH THE BULL: SUNSHINE OR SMOKESCREEN?]**

**[HOST ON CAMERA]**

Welcome back to *Cutting through the Bull*. 

If there’s one word politicians in Washington love to throw around like confetti, it’s "transparency." Every candidate running for office promises to fling open the doors of government, drag backroom deals into the light, and make sure *you*—the voter—know exactly what your elected officials are doing. 

It sounds great on the campaign trail. But once they get the keys to the city? That sunshine turns into a fog real fast.

Let’s cut through the bull and talk about how both parties routinely treat government transparency not as a sacred principle, but as a temporary inconvenience.

**[GRAPHIC: FLASHBACK: 2008 CAMPAIGN TRAIL]**

**[HOST V/O - OVER B-ROLL OF BARACK OBAMA 2008 CAMPAIGN]**

Cast your mind back to 2008. Then-Senator Barack Obama ran on a bold, refreshing pledge. He promised that as President, he would not sign *any* non-emergency legislation into law until it had been posted online for public review for five full days. 

Five days. Five days for journalists, policy experts, and everyday citizens to read the fine print, catch the hidden earmarks, and hold power accountable. It was a flagship promise of a campaign built on "hope and change."

**[HOST ON CAMERA]**

So, what happened when Candidate Obama became President Obama? 

**[GRAPHIC: PROMISE VS. REALITY - THE 5-DAY PLEDGE]**

Well, the bull walked right through the front door. Just days into his administration, President Obama signed the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act. A noble piece of legislation? Many argued yes. But was it posted online for five days before signing? No. 

Shortly after came the massive Children’s Health Insurance reauthorization, and then the nearly $800 billion Economic Stimulus package. Major, transformative bills—signed without giving the public their promised five-day window. 

The White House offered excuses: "procedural deadlines," "urgent economic crises." But the pattern was set. The five-day transparency pledge wasn't a firm rule; it was a PR slogan that collapsed under the slightest political pressure.

**[GRAPHIC: SUNLIGHT FOUNDATION: THE 72-HOUR RULE]**

And this isn't just a White House problem. It’s a Capitol Hill epidemic. 

For years, government watchdog groups—most notably the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation—begged Congress to adopt a basic, commonsense fix: the **72-hour rule**. 

The Sunlight Foundation’s proposal was simple. Before Congress votes on *any* final legislation, the text must be available online, in a searchable format, for at least 72 hours. 

Think about that. Three days. That’s not a high bar. It’s the bare minimum required for a 2,000-page omnibus bill dropped at 2:00 AM on a Thursday so lawmakers—and the public—can actually read what’s in it before a vote at noon on Friday.

**[HOST ON CAMERA]**

So, did Congress embrace the Sunlight Foundation's 72-hour proposal? 

Of course not. Because in Washington, speed and secrecy are political weapons. If the public has 72 hours to read a bill, they might find the special interest favors, the pork-barrel spending, or the unconstitutional tweaks hidden on page 1,402. 

Leaders in both parties—Democrats and Republicans alike—prefer to force votes under the threat of government shutdowns, handing members bills so thick they’d choke a paper shredder, demanding they "vote now and read later."

**[GRAPHIC: CUTTING THROUGH THE BULL: THE BOTTOM LINE]**

Here is the bottom line: Transparency isn't hard to achieve. The technology exists. The proposals, like the Sunlight Foundation's, are ready to go. 

When politicians tell you they can't make bills public for 72 hours—or hold to a 5-day review period—that’s not a technical failure. That’s a political choice. They don't want you to see the process, because if you saw the process, you might not like the product.

And *that* is pure, unadulterated bull.

Up next, we’ll look at...

**[FADE TO COMMERCIAL]**

**MARCUS VANCE (ON CAMERA):**
Good evening. 

"Sunshine is the best disinfectant." It’s a phrase coined over a century ago by Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis, and it became the rallying cry for politicians in 2008. We were promised a new era of open government—a world where bills would sit online for days before a vote, where backroom deals would be replaced by public debate, and where the American taxpayer would see every gear turning in the legislative machine.

But then, reality hit. Panic set in. And in Washington, panic is the ultimate enemy of transparency.

Over the past fourteen months, we have witnessed a historic wave of fast-tracked, hyper-complex legislation. From the final months of the Bush administration through the opening act of the Obama presidency, the mandate from Capitol Hill has been clear: *Act now, read later.* 

**[GRAPHIC: TARP (2008) – $700 BILLION]**

Let’s retrace the steps. It began in the terrifying autumn of 2008 with the Troubled Asset Relief Program—TARP. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson initially presented Congress with a bare-bones, three-page request for $700 billion. Within days, under the ominous threat of total global financial meltdown, that proposal expanded into a massive, 450-page legislative engine. 

Lawmakers were given mere hours to digest a bill that fundamentally reshaped the relationship between the federal government and Wall Street. Representatives openly admitted on the House floor that they hadn't read the whole thing. The promise of public oversight was crushed by the clock. And the immediate result? Months of public confusion, secret institution bailouts, and an auditing nightmare that took years for the Special Inspector General to untangle. Speed won. Transparency lost.

**[CAMERA CUT TO MEDIUM CLOSE-UP]**

**MARCUS VANCE:**
Fast forward to early 2009. A new administration takes office, reiterating its pledge to post bills online for five days before the President signs them. 

Then came the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act—the $787 billion stimulus bill.

**[GRAPHIC: THE STIMULUS BILL – 1,074 PAGES]**

Now, emergency stimulus is a defensible policy goal during a Great Recession. But the *process* was a direct violation of the transparency promise. The final, 1,074-page compromise bill was filed at 11:00 PM on a Thursday night. Members of Congress voted on it the very next afternoon. 

How can the public—or even their elected representatives—hold a government accountable when a trillion-dollar legislative expenditure is passed before the ink is literally dry? The promised five-day public review window wasn't just shortened; it was completely abandoned. The defense was "emergency expediency." The cost was public trust.

**[GRAPHIC: LILLY LEDBETTER FAIR PAY ACT (2009)]**

And it wasn't just massive spending bills. Look at the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act—the very first bill signed into law by President Obama in January 2009. 

Substantively, the bill enjoyed broad popular support aimed at correcting wage discrimination. But procedurally, it was rushed to the President's desk as a political statement of speed and decisive action. By fast-tracking the bill through committee and curtailing floor debate, Congress bypassed crucial public hearings regarding how the law's altered statutes of limitations would affect small businesses and retroactively alter decades of corporate record-keeping rules. Even on legislation with noble intentions, the message was sent: process is secondary to momentum.

**[CAMERA CUT TO MAIN ANCHOR DESK]**

**MARCUS VANCE:**
Here is the uncomfortable truth: Fast-tracked legislation creates a dangerous precedent. When speed becomes the default setting for governance, emergency powers slowly become standard operating procedure. 

TARP, the stimulus, and early legislative pushes demonstrated that when Washington wants to move fast, the first thing thrown out the window is the public's right to know. We were promised sunshine. What we got was a series of legislative midnight rushes. 

When you govern in the dark, even good laws carry the shadow of suspicion. And in a democracy, that shadow is a very expensive price to pay for speed.

Back to you, Sarah.

**[SCENE END]**
